title: The 10 Best Benchtop Thickness Planers
subtitle: Benchtop planers for milling rough lumber to thickness, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: A benchtop thickness planer turns rough or uneven boards into flat, parallel stock at the exact thickness you want. We ranked 10 best-sellers from DEWALT, WEN, CRAFTSMAN, JET, RIKON and Cutech on rating, review volume and features (a helical cutterhead, two feed speeds, snipe control and 13-inch capacity). The DEWALT DW735X is the long-running favorite; helical heads cost more but cut quieter and smoother.
data_source: Amazon product listings on the data_captured date. Prices, ratings and review counts change daily; check the listing before relying on a number.

cons: Same price as the DW735X when captured

products.best_for: Woodworkers who want JET-level features for less money.
products.verdict: A helical, two-speed planer with a threaded four-post head, depth gauge and repeat-cut stops, for less than the JET.

products.name: WEN PL1337 Two-Speed 13-Inch Spiral Benchtop Thickness Planer

products.verdict: WEN's two-speed spiral planer: the same 26-insert head as the PL1326 plus a slow 16 ft/min feed for a finer finish.

products.name: CRAFTSMAN 12.25 In. Benchtop Thickness Planer, 15 Amp, Two Knife (CMEW320)
products.best_for: First-time planer buyers milling pine and poplar.
products.verdict: A budget brand-name planer with a two-knife head on ball bearings and reversible high-carbon steel knives.

products.name: Cutech 40700H 12-1/2-Inch Spiral Cutterhead Benchtop Planer with Carbide Inserts
products.best_for: Woodworkers planing hardwoods who hate changing blades.
products.verdict: The only planer here with tungsten carbide inserts, which stay sharp far longer than HSS. Four lead screws minimize snipe, and rollers on top return boards to the front.

products.name: WEN PL1252 15-Amp 12.5-Inch Two-Blade Benchtop Thickness Planer
products.verdict: A basic WEN planer with two reversible blades and a 12.5-inch width for boards up to 6 inches thick.

avoid.name: 13-Inch Benchtop Thickness Planer, 15A Wood Planer with 4 HSS Blades, 2000W All Copper Motor, Overload Protection
avoid.flag: 2,000 W from a 15 A motor; '4 blades' is 2 plus spares
avoid.verdict: The listing's power and blade claims don't add up, and it rates 4.2 stars on 50 reviews. The WEN PL1252 and CRAFTSMAN CMEW320 cost about the same with hundreds more reviews.
reasons: It claims a '15-AMP 2000W' motor. On a 120V outlet, 15 amps is 1,800 watts, so the 2,000 W figure can't be a continuous rating.
The title says '4 HSS Blades', but the bullets describe a 'dual-blade system' and the included-parts list shows 2 spare blades: it's a two-knife planer with a spare set, not a four-knife head.
It has 50 reviews, far fewer than the similarly priced WEN and CRAFTSMAN planers.

buyers_guide.q: Do I need a thickness planer?
buyers_guide.a: If you buy rough or uneven lumber, yes. A planer makes the top face flat and parallel to the bottom and brings boards to an exact thickness. It doesn't flatten a warped board on its own; that's a jointer's job, or a planer sled.

Straight knives (two or three long blades) are cheaper and fine for pine and poplar. Helical or spiral heads use many small inserts that cut with a shearing action, so they're quieter, tear out less on figured wood, and you rotate one nicked insert instead of replacing a whole knife.

Snipe is a slightly deeper cut at the start or end of a board. Carriage locks, four-post heads and infeed/outfeed tables reduce it. You can also feed boards end to end or leave them long and cut the ends off.
A slower feed takes more cuts per inch for a smoother finish on hardwood. DEWALT's DW735 goes from 96 to 179 cuts per inch on its slow setting. For softwood and rough stock, one speed is fine.
Planers make a lot of chips. Hook one to a shop vac with a cyclone separator or a dust collector. The DW735 has a fan that blows chips out, but it still needs a hose.
